# Training a supervised behaviour classifier {#sec-classification}

In @sec-boris we used BORIS to annotate `mount` events on the video
`mouse044_task1_annotator1.mp4`. In this chapter we put those annotations to work:
we train a **supervised behaviour classifier** that learns to flag `mount` frames
automatically from features derived from the pose tracks.

We will use `movement` to derive the features, and `scikit-learn` to train a simple random forest classifier.
Both packages are included in the `animals-in-motion-env` environment (see
[@sec-install-movement]), so make sure you have that environment activated before proceeding.
We also need the fully annotated SLEAP file (`mouse044_task1_annotator1.slp`) containing pose tracks
and the BORIS ground-truth annotations (`mouse044_task1_mount_events_boris.tsv`) (see [@sec-data]).

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    video[/"Video"/] --SLEAP-->poses[/"Pose tracks"/]
    poses --movement--> feat[Kinematic<br>features]
    video --"BORIS"--> labels[Behaviour<br>annotations]
    feat --train--> model
    labels --train--> model[Random<br>Forest]
```

::: {.callout-note}
The goal here is to teach the **workflow and the main concepts**, not to train a
production-grade classifier. We deliberately use a single annotated video and a
handful of interpretable features. A good model would need far more data, as we
discuss at the end.
:::

## Load pose tracks and annotations

We start by loading the two ingredients of our classifier: the **pose tracks** produced
by SLEAP in @sec-sleap, and the **behaviour annotations** we exported from BORIS in
@sec-boris.

```{python}
#| include: false
import xarray as xr

xr.set_options(
    display_expand_attrs=False,
    display_expand_coords=False,
    keep_attrs=True,
)
```

Let's load the pose tracks into a `movement` dataset with
[`load_dataset()`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.io.load_dataset.html),
just as we did in @sec-movement-load.

```{python}
from pathlib import Path

from movement.io import load_dataset

# Adjust this path if your CalMS21 folder lives elsewhere
data_dir = Path.home() / ".movement" / "CalMS21"

ds = load_dataset(
    data_dir / "mouse044_task1_annotator1.slp",
    source_software="SLEAP",
    fps=30,
)
ds
```

Since these annotations have been generated by manual labeling, their confidence is undefined (`nan`) for all frames.
This means we can skip most common filtering steps, but we will still apply a short smoothing filter to reduce jitter in the tracks;
human labelers suffer from the same frame-to-frame jitter as pose estimation algorithms.

```{python}
from movement.filtering import rolling_filter

ds.update(
  {"position": rolling_filter(ds.position, window=7, min_periods=2)}
)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Updating in-place" collapse="true"}
Here we updated the existing `position` data variable in-place, effectively overwriting the original position information with the smoothed data. Depending on your specific workflow, you may prefer to create a new variable instead, or store the smoothed positions as a standalone data array.

```{.python}
# Add a new variable to the same dataset
ds["position_smoothed"] = rolling_filter(ds.position, window=5, min_periods)

# or, store the resulting data array in a separate variable
position_smoothed = ds.position_smoothed
```

:::

Next, we load the BORIS annotations, in a format you've already seen in @sec-boris: one row per `mount` bout, columns separated by tabs.

```{python}
import pandas as pd

boris_df = pd.read_csv(
    data_dir / "mouse044_task1_mount_events_boris.tsv", sep="\t"
)
columns_of_interest = [
    "Subject", "Behavior", "Start (s)", "Stop (s)",
    "Duration (s)", "Image index start", "Image index stop",
]
boris_df[columns_of_interest]
```

## Add per-frame labels

BORIS gives us one row per `mount` bout, with a start and stop frame. To use these
as training labels we expand them into a **per-frame boolean array**,
`True` while a mount is ongoing and `False` otherwise.
We can store this array in the dataset as a new **data variable**, alongside `position` and
`confidence`, so the labels travel together with the tracks.
This is our label vector `y`,
i.e. the ground truth we want the classifier to learn to predict.

```{python}
# Start with an all-False boolean array the size of dataset's time axis
ds["is_mount"] = xr.zeros_like(ds.time, dtype=bool)

# Fill in True between start and stop frames for each BORIS bout
for _, ev in boris_df.iterrows():
  start, stop = ev["Image index start"], ev["Image index stop"]
  ds["is_mount"][{"time": slice(start, stop)}] = True

ds.is_mount
```

Let's calculate the fraction of frames that are `mount`.

```{python}
mount_fraction = ds.is_mount.mean()
print(f"Mount frames: {mount_fraction.item():.2%}")
```

::: {.callout-note title="Why did we use the mean?" collapse="true"}
Computing a fraction involves summing up the number of values and dividing by the total length of an array.
Because `True` is treated as `1` and `False` as `0`, the mean of a boolean array gives exactly this fraction.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Discuss"}
We have much fewer `mount` frames than `non-mount` frames.
This situation—often referred to as **class imbalance**—is quite common in behaviour classification scenarios.
Why could that be a problem for training and evaluating a classifier?
:::

## Our first classifier: a distance threshold

A classifier can only be as good as the data we give it.
In machine learning terms, the data variables we feed into the model are called **features**.

Rather than throwing raw keypoint coordinates at the model, let's derive a small set of **interpretable features**,
each motivated by what mounting actually looks like in the resident–intruder assay.

*What would be a good set of features to distinguish `mount` from `non-mount` frames?*

Let's start with an obvious one: the **distance between the two mice**.
During a mount, the resident is on top of the intruder, so their centroids should be very close together.

We compute the inter-mouse distance (as we did in @sec-movement-intro).

```{python}
from movement.kinematics import compute_pairwise_distances

centroid_pos = ds.position.mean("keypoint")  # one point per mouse
inter_mouse_distance = compute_pairwise_distances(
    centroid_pos,
    dim="individual",
    pairs={"resident_b": "intruder_w"},
)
inter_mouse_distance
```

Let's plot it across time, while highlighting the `mount` frames (expand the code block if you want to see the plotting function).

```{python}
#| label: fig-inter-mouse-distance
#| fig-cap: "Inter-mouse distance over time, with mount frames highlighted."
#| code-fold: true

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def plot_over_time(data_array, mount, ylabel, ymax=None):
    """Plot a per-frame quantity over time, with mount frames highlighted.

    ``mount`` is a boolean array (aligned to ``data_array``'s time axis) marking
    the frames to shade.
    """
    ymax = float(data_array.max()) if ymax is None else ymax
    plt.figure(figsize=(7, 3))
    plt.plot(data_array.time, data_array)
    plt.fill_between(
        data_array.time, 0, ymax,
        where=mount, color="orange", edgecolor=None, alpha=0.3,
    )
    plt.xlabel("time (s)")
    plt.ylabel(ylabel)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

plot_over_time(inter_mouse_distance, ds.is_mount, ylabel="distance (px)")
```

That looks very promising: the inter-mouse distance is clearly low during mounts.

How far can this single feature take us? Let's turn the inter-mouse distance into a simple yes/no rule by choosing an arbitrary threshold of 100 pixels (based on eye-balling the above plot), and see how well it separates the two classes.

```{python}
distance_threshold = 100  # pixels

ds["predicted_mount"] = inter_mouse_distance < distance_threshold
ds.predicted_mount
```

This single rule is already a "classifier", if a crude one.
To see how good it is, we compare its predictions against the ground-truth labels.
A **confusion matrix** is the clearest place to start: it counts how many frames fall into each combination of predicted vs. actual state.
We normalise the counts per row (`normalize="true"`), so every *true* class sums to 100%.

```{python}
#| label: fig-threshold-confusion
#| fig-cap: "Row-normalised confusion matrix for the distance-threshold baseline (all frames)."
from sklearn.metrics import ConfusionMatrixDisplay

ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_predictions(
    ds.is_mount.values,
    ds.predicted_mount.values,
    display_labels=["not mount", "mount"],
    normalize="true",      # normalise over each true-class row
    values_format=".0%",
    cmap="magma",
)
plt.show()
```

To boil these results down to a few numbers, we use `scikit-learn`'s
[`classification_report`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.metrics.classification_report.html),
which reports **precision**, **recall** and **F1-score** for each class.

```{python}
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report

print(classification_report(
    ds.is_mount.values,
    ds.predicted_mount.values,
    target_names=["not mount", "mount"],
))
```

::: {.callout-note title="Understanding the classification report" collapse="true"}
All metrics are built from just four counts, obtained by comparing predictions
against the ground truth. Taking `mount` as the "positive" class:

- **TP** (true positives): `mount` frames correctly predicted as `mount`.
- **FP** (false positives): `non-mount` frames wrongly predicted as `mount`.
- **TN** (true negatives): `non-mount` frames correctly predicted as `non-mount`.
- **FN** (false negatives): `mount` frames wrongly predicted as `non-mount`.

These are exactly the four cells of the confusion matrix above. From them:

**Precision** (a.k.a. *positive predictive value*): of everything flagged as `mount`, what fraction really was?
$$\text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}$$

**Recall** (a.k.a. *sensitivity*, *true positive rate*, *hit rate*): of all true `mount` frames, what fraction did we catch?
$$\text{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}$$

**F1 score**: the harmonic mean of precision and recall; high only when *both* are high.
$$F_1 = 2 \cdot \frac{\text{Precision} \cdot \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}} = \frac{2\,TP}{2\,TP + FP + FN}$$

**Accuracy**: the fraction of *all* frames classified correctly. Simple, but easily
inflated when one class dominates (see below).
$$\text{Accuracy} = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + TN + FP + FN}$$
:::

Focusing on the `mount` class:

- **Recall ≈ 0.76** — of all true `mount` frames, the distance rule catches about three-quarters.
- **Precision ≈ 0.58** — of all frames it *labels* `mount`, only ~58% really are, so roughly 40% are false alarms.
- **F1 ≈ 0.66** — the harmonic mean of the two, a convenient single-number summary that balances the two types of mistakes.

That is remarkably good for a one-line rule! But look at what **accuracy** (0.84) hides.

::: {.callout-warning title="Accuracy can be misleading"}
Only ~21% of frames are mounts, so a lazy classifier that *always* predicts "not mount"
would already score ~79% accuracy—while catching zero mounts. Our threshold scores only a
little higher on accuracy, yet it actually finds most of the mounts. For imbalanced
problems like this, precision, recall and F1 are far more informative than accuracy alone.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Discuss"}
In real life, we will want to analyse more than 1.5 minutes of video, and we will want to apply the classifier to new videos.
So let's think about generalisation:

- Do you expect the above threshold to generalise well to a new video? Why or why not?
- How would you go about picking the threshold more systematically, rather than by eye?
:::

## Adding more features

One feature and a hand-tuned threshold already got us surprisingly far, but that's not going to be good enough.
There are many situations—other than the resident mounting the intruder—in which the two mice are close together.
For example:

- the intruder could be mounting the resident.
- they could be interacting in other ways (sniffing, fighting, play).

We don't have many such examples in this single video, but we are likely to encounter them in new videos.

One way to improve the classifier is to add more features so the model can learn a more nuanced decision boundary than a single yes/no threshold.

Conceptually, can can think of each additional feature as a new yes/no question the model can ask about each frame, e.g. "are the mice close together?", "is the intruder facing away from the resident?", "is the resident moving fast?", etc. That's the exact intuition behind **tree-based models** like random forests: each **tree** is a series of yes/no questions that splits the data into smaller and smaller subsets (branches), ideally until each *leaf* contains only one class.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-decision-tree
%%| fig-cap: "A decision tree is just a cascade of simple threshold questions."
graph TD
    q1{"Are the mice close?<br/>distance &lt; 100 px"}
    q1 -->|no| n1["not mount"]
    q1 -->|yes| q2{"Is the intruder<br/>facing away?<br/>angle &gt; 90 deg"}
    q2 -->|no| n2["not mount"]
    q2 -->|yes| m1["mount"]

    classDef mount fill:#3182bd,stroke:#08519c,color:#ffffff;
    classDef notmount fill:#eeeeee,stroke:#bbbbbb,color:#000000;
    class m1 mount;
    class n1,n2 notmount;
```

So let's compute a few more **interpretable** features—each motivated by what
mounting actually looks like in the resident–intruder assay.

We've seen in the video that mounting typically involves the resident being on top and behind the intruder, while the intruder is facing away.
This suggests that **orientation** features could be useful, in addition to the inter-mouse distance we already have.
Let's compute one such feature with `movement`: the **intruder-facing-resident angle**.

We'll do that in two steps:

1. Compute the vector pointing from the intruder's centroid to the resident's centroid.
2. Compute the angle between that vector and the intruder's forward-facing direction, using `compute_forward_vector_angle()`.

```{python}
from movement.kinematics import compute_forward_vector_angle

resident_c = centroid_pos.sel(individual="resident_b")  # resident centroid
intruder_c = centroid_pos.sel(individual="intruder_w")  # intruder centroid
intruder = ds.position.sel(individual="intruder_w")     # intruder keypoints (for its facing direction)

# We derive the vector by subtracting the centroids
intruder_to_resident_vector = resident_c - intruder_c

# We compute intruder's forward-facing angle
# relative to the vector pointing to the resident
intruder_facing_resident_angle = compute_forward_vector_angle(
    data=intruder,
    left_keypoint="left_ear",
    right_keypoint="right_ear",
    camera_view="top_down",
    reference_vector=intruder_to_resident_vector,
    in_degrees=True
)
intruder_facing_resident_angle
```

::: {.callout-tip title="How does `compute_forward_vector_angle()` work?" collapse="true"}
Explain with schematics from movement head direction example.
:::

This is a signed angle, with 0° meaning the intruder is facing directly at the resident, and ±180° meaning it is facing directly away.
Here we don't care about the sign, so we take the absolute value to get a range from 0° to 180°.

```{python}
intruder_facing_resident_angle = abs(intruder_facing_resident_angle)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-intruder-facing-resident-angle
#| fig-cap: "Intruder-facing-resident angle over time, with mount frames highlighted."
#| code-fold: true
plot_over_time(intruder_facing_resident_angle, ds.is_mount, ylabel="angle (deg)", ymax=180)
```

Our intuition is confirmed: during many mounts the angle is near 180°,
meaning the intruder is facing away from the resident.

Let's add one last feature: the resident's centroid **speed**.
During a mount, the resident is relatively stationary—hunched over the intruder rather than
travelling across the arena—so its speed should be low. We compute it from the resident
centroid with [`compute_speed`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.kinematics.compute_speed.html).

```{python}
from movement.kinematics import compute_speed

resident_speed = compute_speed(resident_c)
resident_speed
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-resident-speed
#| fig-cap: "Resident speed over time, with mount frames highlighted."
#| code-fold: true
plot_over_time(resident_speed, ds.is_mount, ylabel="speed (px/s)")
```

The signal here is weaker than for the other two features: the resident does tend to slow
down during mounts, but it also slows down at plenty of other times, so speed alone would
make a poor classifier. It may still help the model in combination with distance and
orientation though.

We now have three features. Following the `scikit-learn` convention, we collect them into a
feature matrix `X`—one row per frame, one column per feature—alongside the label vector `y`
(our `is_mount` ground truth).

```{python}
X = pd.DataFrame({
    "inter_mouse_distance": inter_mouse_distance.values,
    "intruder_facing_resident_angle": intruder_facing_resident_angle.values,
    "resident_speed": resident_speed.values,
})
y = ds.is_mount.values

X.head()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Discuss"}

- Here we hand-picked three features that we thought would be useful. What are the pros and cons of this approach?
- What if we were trying to distinguish between many different behaviours, not just `mount` vs `non-mount`?
- Why don't we just feed the raw keypoint coordinates into the model and let it figure out the features itself?
:::

## What is a random forest?

As feature numbers grow, it's no longer practical to eyeball each one individually and hand-pick thresholds.
Instead, we will let a machine learning model to learn the best decision boundary from the data.
Specifically, we will train a **random forest classifier** which is a type of ensemble model that combines many decision trees to make predictions.

As we mentioned above, each **tree** is a cascade of yes/no questions about the features.
Intuitevely, the **forest** aggregates votes from multiple trees to make a final prediction.
The **random** part comes from training each tree on a random subset of the data and features, which helps to reduce overfitting and improve generalisation.

Random forests are an excellent starting point: they are robust, require little tuning, and can handle features on different scales (pixels, radians, pixels/second) without the need for normalization. Moreover, there are easy-to-train without consuming too much time or computational resources.

Learn more about [decision trees](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/tree.html) and [random forests](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/ensemble.html#forest) in the `scikit-learn` documentation.

## Train / validation split

We split the single video **in time**: train on roughly the first 70% of frames,
validate on the last ~30%.

::: {.callout-important title="Why not a random split?"}
Adjacent frames are almost identical, so a *random* split would put near-duplicate
frames in both sets. The model would appear to score brilliantly while having
essentially memorised its neighbours — **information leakage**. A temporal split keeps
train and validation genuinely separate.

Note the naming: this held-out tail is a **validation** set, not a test set. As soon as
we inspect its scores and adjust features or thresholds to improve them, it has
influenced our choices. The honest **test** comes later, on a brand-new video
the model never saw (see [The real test](#the-real-test-a-new-video) below).
:::

```{python}
split = int(0.7 * len(X))
X_train, X_val = X.iloc[:split], X.iloc[split:]
y_train, y_val = y[:split], y[split:]

print(f"Train:      {len(X_train)} frames ({y_train.sum()} mount)")
print(f"Validation: {len(X_val)} frames ({y_val.sum()} mount)")

# A temporal split only works if mounts fall on *both* sides of the cut.
# This is not guaranteed in general, so we check it explicitly.
assert y_train.sum() > 0 and y_val.sum() > 0, "A split has no mount frames!"
```

Both splits contain mount bouts, so the model has positive examples to learn from and we
have some to evaluate on. This is worth checking rather than assuming: a purely temporal
split gives no guarantee that the rare behaviour appears on both sides of the cut. Here
it does, because this video happens to have mounts near the end. With a different video—or
a behaviour that only occurs early—you might need to choose the split point more carefully,
or reserve a whole separate video for validation.

::: {.callout-tip title="Splitting across videos"}
We split a single video in time only because we have just one annotated video here. When
you have **several** annotated videos, the cleaner approach is to split *across* videos:
train on some, validate on others. This keeps all frames from any given video on one side
of the split, avoiding the frame-to-frame leakage that motivated our temporal split in the
first place—and it better reflects the real goal of generalising to *new* videos.
:::

## Train a random forest

We're finally ready to train. A
[`RandomForestClassifier`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestClassifier.html)
is a solid, low-fuss baseline for tabular features: it needs little tuning and copes well
with features on different scales (pixels, radians, pixels/second). We set
`class_weight="balanced"` so the rare `mount` class is not swamped by the majority, and
fix `random_state` for reproducibility.

```{python}
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

clf = RandomForestClassifier(class_weight="balanced", random_state=0)
clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
```

That's it—`clf` is now a trained classifier. Training on a few thousand frames with three
features takes barely a moment.

## Evaluate on the validation set

Now we ask the model to predict `mount` on the held-out validation frames and compare
against the ground truth. For an imbalanced problem, we look at **precision, recall and
F1** for the `mount` class rather than plain accuracy.

::: {.callout-warning title="Accuracy lies under imbalance"}
A classifier that *never* predicts mount would still be correct on all 848 non-mount
frames in our validation set—about **83% accuracy**—while catching not a single one of the
171 mounts. Accuracy alone would call that useless model a success. Precision and recall
tell the real story.
:::

```{python}
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report

y_pred = clf.predict(X_val)
print(classification_report(y_val, y_pred, target_names=["not mount", "mount"]))
```

A confusion matrix shows *where* the mistakes fall—false positives (non-mount frames
flagged as mount) versus false negatives (missed mounts).

```{python}
#| label: fig-confusion-matrix
#| fig-cap: "Confusion matrix on the validation set"
from sklearn.metrics import ConfusionMatrixDisplay

ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_predictions(
    y_val, y_pred, display_labels=["not mount", "mount"], cmap="Blues"
)
plt.show()
```

The scores are **modest**—recall around 0.70 means we still miss about 30% of mount frames,
and precision around 0.67 means roughly a third of predicted mount frames are false alarms.
That's about what we should expect from three hand-picked features and a single training
video; the point here is the *workflow*, not the numbers. We'll recover some of the ragged
edges in the next section by smoothing predictions into bouts.

Finally, we can ask the model which features it leaned on most.

```{python}
#| label: fig-feature-importances
#| fig-cap: "Random forest feature importances"
importances = pd.Series(
    clf.feature_importances_, index=X.columns
).sort_values()

importances.plot.barh()
plt.xlabel("importance")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

As the exploratory plots suggested, **inter-mouse distance** dominates, with the
**intruder-facing angle** a clear second. **Resident speed** ranks last—consistent with the
weak signal we saw in @fig-resident-speed—yet the model still makes some use of it.

::: {.callout-note title="Take feature importances with a pinch of salt" collapse="true"}
The importances reported by a random forest are *impurity-based*, and this measure is
known to inflate the apparent importance of continuous, high-cardinality features (like
our distances and angles) relative to coarse ones. It's a useful rough guide to what the
model uses, but not a rigorous ranking. More reliable alternatives, such as
[permutation importance](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/permutation_importance.html),
measure how much performance drops when a feature is shuffled.
:::

## From frame predictions to behaviour bouts

Per-frame predictions are noisy (isolated flipped frames). We **post-process** them
into clean bouts: fill short gaps, drop very short detections, then overlay the
predicted bouts against the BORIS ground-truth bouts on a timeline. This connects back
to the bout-style annotations from @sec-boris.

```{.python}
# smooth predictions -> merge into [start, stop] bouts -> timeline plot vs ground truth
```

## The real test: a new video

Now we apply the trained model to a **different** video it has never seen — with its own
BORIS ground-truth annotations (provided). We compute the same features, predict, and
compare.

Use mouse0026 (already locally), make sure to put on dropbox and pre-requisites.

Expect the scores to **drop** relative to validation. That gap is the honest measure of
how well the model generalises, and a teaching moment in itself: differences in lighting,
animals, and behaviour between videos (**domain shift**), combined with training on a
single video and few positive examples, all hurt generalisation.

```{.python}
# load new video's tracks + BORIS labels -> same feature pipeline -> clf.predict -> metrics
```

## Good practice, limitations, and where to go next

What we would do to build a classifier worth trusting:

- **More data**: many videos, multiple animals, and ideally multiple annotators (and
  measure inter-annotator agreement).
- **Better validation**: cross-validation that splits by *video*, never mixing frames
  from one video across folds.
- **Richer features**: compute many diverse features — closer to how tools like SimBA, MARS and JABS operate.
- **Use more than just the current frame**: I think CalMS21 paper may have a good figure on this.
- **Handle imbalance** deliberately (class weights, resampling, threshold tuning on the
  precision/recall trade-off).
- **Off-the-shelf tools** built for this: [SimBA](https://github.com/sgoldenlab/simba),
  [MARS](https://github.com/neuroethology/MARS),
  [DeepEthogram](https://github.com/jbohnslav/deepethogram),
  [keypoint-MoSeq](https://keypoint-moseq.readthedocs.io/), and
  [A-SOiD](https://github.com/YttriLab/A-SOID).
- **Different architectures**: sequence models like RNNs and Transformers that can learn from the temporal structure of behaviour.
- **Diffrenet features source**: models like FERAL for direct video-to-behaviour classification, or sequence models like RNNs and Transformers that can learn from the temporal structure of behaviour.
